newsitem.title: UK: STABLE EARNINGS SHOW UK LABOUR MARKET STILL SLACK.
newsitem.headline: STABLE EARNINGS SHOW UK LABOUR MARKET STILL SLACK.

text.p: A unexpectedly sharp fall in British unemployment in July should not start inflation alarm bells ringing just yet as stable average earnings suggest there is still some slack in the labour market, analysts said on Wednesday.

"The pace of decline in jobless at this point in the economic cycle would normally give rise to concern over wage pressures, but markets will be reassured at the behaviour of earnings so far this year," said CIBC Wood Gundy chief economist David Coleman.
Data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) released on Wednesday showed a larger-than-expected tumble of 49,800 in jobless numbers in July, against expectations of around 31,000.
Average earnings, an important barometer of future inflationary trends, remained steady in the year to June at 4.25 percent.

"The labour market is tight, but I still think there's some spare capacity. There is going to be a point at which the falls in unemployment does start to trigger wage pressures, but I think we're some way from that just now," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
The jobless rate fell to 5.5 percent from 5.7 percent in June, and the level of unemployed fell to 1.55 million, the lowest level since September 1980.
The ONS said much of this month's slide in jobless figures could be attributed to the fact that fewer school leavers than usual were signing up for unemployment benefits.
The strong continuing fall in the jobless rate indicates the British economy is still thriving, but steady earnings growth suggests inflationary pressures are not making themselves felt yet.
Economists also pointed out it was worth looking at the employment figures for a more complete picture of the labour market.

"You can't just look at unemployment, you also need to look at the other side of the equation -- which is employment. Employment has been picking up but the unemployment data still overstates the tightness of the labour market," Stamenkovic said.
Analysts compared the British labour market to its counterpart in the United States, which enjoys strong activity, falling unemployment and subdued wages growth in tandem with low inflation.
But they said that a continued fall in jobless numbers, even with no evidence of rising wage pressures, was likely to make the Bank of England look carefully at interest rates in the future.

"The members of the (Bank of England) Monetary Policy Committee will be concerned that unemployment cannot keep falling this fast without wage pressures eventually emerging," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
"Accordingly, while interest rates are on hold for a while, they have probably not yet reached a peak."

The Bank raised interest rates a fourth time in as many months last week, pushing them up to 7.0 percent and said in its quarterly inflation report on Wednesday it would now pause for breath as rates were consistent with its 2.5 percent two-year inflation target.
But it also voiced concerns about the tightening in labour market conditions, warning that further rises in earnings growth could reduce the chances of meeting the inflation target.
"Obviously there's going to be a point at which the fall in unemployment rates does start to trigger wage pressures, but I think we're some way from that just yet," DKB's Stamenkovic said.
